note: Reviews student and teacher assistance, adaptive learning and commercial tools, with the datasets and benchmarks behind each, plus the deployment risks.
title: Large Language Models for Education: A survey and outlook

reading.body:
This survey reviews how language models are used to assist students and teachers, covering adaptive learning tools, the datasets and benchmarks used to evaluate them, and the deployment risks involved.

Education is one of the sectors where AI adoption is furthest from a compute or infrastructure story and closest to a pedagogy story, since the tools reviewed here are mostly about personalizing instruction and supporting teachers rather than automating a task outright. The inclusion of commercial tools alongside research systems suggests the gap between lab research and classroom deployment in this sector is relatively narrow compared to other fields.

The survey does not report original outcome data on whether these tools improve learning, only that it catalogs what has been built and what risks researchers have flagged.

explain_beginner: This survey looks at how the AI language models behind tools like ChatGPT are already being built into products used by students and teachers, not just discussed as a future possibility. It groups real existing tools into categories, chatbot tutors that answer student questions any time of day, platforms that help teachers create lesson plans and grade work faster, and systems that try to adjust material to each student's level automatically. The authors list dozens of named products already on the market and the datasets researchers use to test how well these systems actually teach or grade. Alongside the promise, they flag specific problems already showing up in classrooms, tools that confidently state wrong facts, students leaning on AI so much they stop practicing writing or problem solving themselves, and unequal access for students who speak languages the tools support less well. The survey does not resolve which of these tools genuinely improve learning outcomes, it maps out what exists and what needs studying next.
explain_business: Education technology buyers and school administrators evaluating an LLM based product can use this survey's categorization, tutoring, teacher productivity, or adaptive learning, to identify which category of existing tool actually matches their intended use case rather than treating all AI in education products as interchangeable. The specific risks flagged, particularly the unresolved student data privacy question and the documented tendency for over reliance to most affect already disadvantaged learners, are directly relevant to procurement and equity policy right now, since these tools are already deployed at scale in classrooms. Institutions adopting these systems should ask vendors directly what data is retained on student interactions, since the authors note this remains underexplored industry wide, and should budget for teacher oversight rather than assuming automated grading or tutoring tools can run unsupervised from day one.
explain_practitioner: This survey catalogs LLM based education tools across student support, teacher support, and adaptive learning, naming specific deployed systems such as Khanmigo for tutoring, MagicSchool with over 40 tools for lesson planning and grading, Curipod for interactive slide generation, and assessment tools like Quizizz AI and Formative, alongside benchmark datasets used to evaluate underlying task performance, including GSM8K and MATH for quantitative reasoning, MedQA for domain question answering, and grammar correction sets such as CoNLL-2014 and BEA-2019. The authors organize identified risks into distinct categories rather than one general concern, hallucination in generated content, demographic and language bias disadvantaging non-English speakers, academic integrity threats from undetectable AI written work, and an underexplored student data privacy problem around what these platforms log and retain. Their stated future direction is to move toward retrieval augmented, pedagogically aligned models rather than assuming general purpose chat models are sufficient for instructional use as they stand today.
